newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Annan proposes phased U.N. exit from E. Slavonia.
newsitem.headline: Annan proposes phased U.N. exit from E. Slavonia.

text.p: Secretary-General Kofi Annan recommended on Wednesday a two-phase "exit strategy" for the withdrawal of a U.N. operation that has been overseeing the reintegration of the heavily Serb-inhabited region of Eastern Slavonia into Croatia.

In a written report to the Security Council, he said the pace of the handover to Croatian control would be commensurate with Croatia's performance in reassuring the Serb population and peacefully reintegrating the region.

The current mandate of the U.N. Transitional Administration for Eastern Slavonia (UNTAES), which includes some 5,000 troops, expires on July 15. Under the 1995 Dayton peace accords a U.N. presence could remain until Jan. 15, 1998.
Annan said that while the "institutional reintegration of the territory into the region is being finalised ... the reintegration of the people has hardly begun."
In the first phase of the proposed withdrawal the number of U.N. troops would be halved by mid-August.

Transitional Administrator Jacques Paul Klein of the United States would also "devolve to Croatia executive responsibility for the major part of civil administration of the region whilst maintaining his authority and ability to intervene and overrule decisions should the situation deteriorate and the achievements of UNTAES be threatened."
"The pace of devolution would be commensurate with Croatia's demonstrated ability to reassure the Serb population and successfully complete peaceful reintegration," the secretary-general said.

"In the second phase, and subject to satisfactory Croatian performance, remaining executive functions would be devolved, with Croatia assuming responsibility for the continued demilitarization of the region and the gradual integration of the Transitional Police Force into the Croatian police force."
Under this arrangement, UNTAES personnel and resources would be reduced progressively as executive functions were assumed by Croatian authorities.
In the first phase, two battalions and one company could be repatriated by Aug. 15, reducing the troop strength from 5,000 to 2,530, including 720 military support personnel.
"Further reductions are planned for the period after September in order to reach a level of 720 by October in the light of developments in the country," Annan said.

The number of military observers would remain at 100 while the authorised strength of 600 civilian police could be reduced to the present actual strength of 450 until the full integration of the Transitional Police Force into the Croatian police force, expected in October.

The civilian police strength could subsequently be further reduced to 250, enabling a constant presence to be maintained at all police stations and two regional headquarters while monitoring the new police structure and continuing human rights training.
By October the strength of UNTAES's civilian component would be reduced from 485 to 315 international staff and from 746 to 399 local staff, apart from 70 U.N. volunteers.

Annan said the essential prerequisite was the "full cooperation of the Croatian government which bears the responsibility of convincing the local population that reintegration of the people of the region is sustainable and that the process of reconciliation and return is irreversible."

Croatia still had to demonstrate its determination to fulfil this responsibility, he said, adding: "If confidence is not achieved, the Security Council would have to reassess the situation by October 15, 1997."
